title: How to (Accidentally) Tell Old Money from New Money in Karachi. Tip #1
body: Old Karachi money says "we're in Bath Island" or "Block 4." New money says "Phase 8, near the Creek." One lives in a flat with high ceilings and bad plumbing. The other has a house with a lift. Old money's building has been there since before Khayaban-e-Ittehad was widened. New money's building has a name, a logo, and a brochure. It's a sealed deal when you realise one of them lives in a flat by choice and the other cannot understand why.

title: How to (Accidentally) Tell Old Money from New Money in Karachi. Tip #2
body: Ask about the beach. Old money has a hut at French Beach falling apart since the seventies. New money has a farmhouse past the toll plaza with a pool and a sound system. Both leave the city on Saturday. Only one had to buy anything recently. It's a sealed deal if the hut has no electricity and everybody prefers it that way.

title: How to (Accidentally) Tell Old Money from New Money in Karachi. Tip #3
body: Listen to how KGS gets said. Old money says it once, flat, because everyone at the table already worked it out. New money says the school and then mentions the fee structure. Same information. Entirely different transaction. It's a sealed deal if somebody adds that their mother went there too and finds it unremarkable.

title: How to (Accidentally) Tell Old Money from New Money in Karachi. Tip #4
body: The club splits it instantly. Sindh Club because the grandfather was, and the waiting list is a story other people tell. New money applied in 2015, knows someone on the committee, still waiting. This is the one thing money genuinely cannot accelerate. It's a sealed deal if a family walks in and signs nothing.

title: How to (Accidentally) Tell Old Money from New Money in Karachi. Tip #5
body: Old money drives a 2009 Land Cruiser with a scratch down one side nobody has fixed in six years. New money drives something German, two years old, ceramic coated. The scratch is the flex, because caring is the tell. It's a sealed deal if the old car's driver has worked for that family longer than the new family has had money.

title: How to (Accidentally) Tell Old Money from New Money in Karachi. Tip #6
body: Old money holds the wedding at the house or the club, eight hundred people, food nobody can source. New money books a hotel and the singer's fee circulates for a week. The spend is comparable. The visibility is the entire difference. It's a sealed deal if the same garden has hosted four generations of one family's weddings.

title: How to (Accidentally) Tell Old Money from New Money in Karachi. Tip #7
body: Ask about the business and count the words. Old money says shipping, or textiles, and stops, and the follow-up gets a polite nothing. New money describes a portfolio. One of them owns something. The other is building something, which is harder and less respected and probably more admirable. It's a sealed deal if the second question goes nowhere.

title: How to (Accidentally) Tell Old Money from New Money in Karachi. Tip #8
body: Here's what nobody admits: new money is having a better time. Better parties, better cars, genuine enthusiasm. Old money is in a flat that needs rewiring, being quietly certain, faintly bored. Everyone says they respect the second. Everyone wants the invitation from the first. It's a sealed deal when a family has been wealthy long enough to find it uninteresting.
